newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Vimpel sees subscriber gains.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Vimpel sees subscriber gains.

text.p: Vimpel-Communications Inc, the first Russian company to trade on the New York Stock Exchange, said Friday the number of subscribers to its wireless communications network in Russia is continuing to grow quickly, a trend it expects to sustain.

Chairman Augie Fabela said the company's objective has been to add on average 3,000 subscribers a month, which it has done. As of September 30 the company had some 45,000 users, mainly in the Moscow area, compared with about 35,000 at the end of the second quarter.

"We definitely have been keeping that run rate very comfortably," Fabela said in an interview here. "It's a very fundamental and sound business because there is such a need for telecommunications, just basic communications in Russia."
Vimpel began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on November 15, 1996, surging about 42 percent to 29-1/4 from its offer price of 20-1/2 and surprising most analysts.
The stock has since settled, trading up 5/8 at 24-1/4 on Friday.
"We definitely saw a bit of a normalizing of our price, which we're very comfortable with," Fabela said.
At this point, customers are primarily businesses, with 95 percent Russian and 90 percent of the calls local.
"We thought it would be solely for international and solely for foreigners in the Russian business community and both of those concepts have proven completely wrong," he said.

The Russian business community has taken off in the last five years, but infrastructure, including conventional telephone networks, has been hard-pressed to keep up. Fabela said the lack of international telephone lines and the poor quality of telephone service in Moscow has given Vimpel, the largest wireless telephone company in Russia, its opportunity.
"Growth is being fuelled by the growth of business," Fabela said. "You can't improve the whole telecommunications infrastructure in five years."
At this point, wireless phones have only about one percent penetration, compared with four to five percent in other emerging markets, or 10 to 13 percent in the U.S., Fabela said.
"There is a long way to go," Fabela said, adding that an independent researcher has projected penetration in Russia at four percent by the Year 2000, which some analysts feel is conservative.
"We're just at the tip of the iceberg now as far as what penetration will be," he said. "We think there is a tremendous amount of growth ahead of us."

While high prices have kept most consumers from buying wireless phones, Vimpel will target that market with its new Personal Communications Services system. The system being tested and is on schedule to be fully commercially available during the second half of 1997.

Just to start up service, Vimpel customers currently pay at least $1,800. And that is down from $5,000 when the company first offered service in 1994. But lower prices have kept demand from outgrowing the infrastructure in place.
"We've been able to stay ahead in the past year...in capacity, but not by much, because growth continues to be strong, even at those price levels," Fabela said.
Vimpel will also expand geographically, but stick mainly to areas surrounding Moscow, where the wealth is centered. Expansion could mean acquisitions or partnerships.
"We always want to have a local partner, because having a local presence is always very important," Fabela added.
